question: Does any vessel technically have the 'right-of-way' over another vessel under Georgia's navigation rules?
choice_a: Yes, the larger vessel always has the right-of-way
choice_b: Yes, the vessel that arrives first always has priority
choice_c: No -- even though no vessel has the right-of-way, both operators are equally responsible for taking action needed to avoid a collision
choice_d: Yes, powerboats always have the right-of-way over sailboats
explanation: No vessel technically has the 'right-of-way'; instead, both operators share equal responsibility for taking whatever action is needed to avoid a collision.
source_note: Handbook of Georgia Boating Laws and Responsibilities, 'Encountering Other Vessels'

question: What are the three basic rules of navigation every Georgia boat operator should follow to prevent collisions?
choice_a: Always travel at maximum speed, use only radio communication, and avoid all other vessels entirely
choice_b: Follow only daytime rules; nighttime rules do not apply on lakes
choice_c: Yield only to vessels displaying a flag
choice_d: Practice good seamanship, keep a sharp lookout, and maintain a safe speed and distance
explanation: The three basic rules of navigation are to practice good seamanship, keep a sharp lookout, and maintain a safe speed and distance, all aimed at preventing collisions.
source_note: Handbook of Georgia Boating Laws and Responsibilities, 'Encountering Other Vessels'

question: When two power-driven vessels meet head-on, what should each operator do?
choice_a: Neither is the stand-on vessel; both vessels should keep to the starboard (right)
choice_b: Both vessels should turn to port (left) to pass each other
choice_c: The larger vessel should hold course while the smaller one stops completely
choice_d: Both vessels should immediately reverse engines
explanation: When two power-driven vessels meet head-on, neither is the stand-on vessel; both should keep to the starboard (right) side so they pass safely port-to-port.
source_note: Handbook of Georgia Boating Laws and Responsibilities, 'Navigation Rules -- Meeting Head-On'

question: In a crossing situation between two power-driven vessels, which vessel is the give-way vessel?
choice_a: The vessel on the operator's starboard side is always the give-way vessel
choice_b: The vessel on the operator's port (left) side is the give-way vessel; the vessel on the operator's starboard (right) side is the stand-on vessel
choice_c: Whichever vessel is moving faster is the stand-on vessel
choice_d: Crossing situations have no designated give-way vessel
explanation: In a crossing situation between two power-driven vessels, the vessel that has the other on its own port (left) side is the give-way vessel, while the vessel on the operator's starboard side is the stand-on vessel.
source_note: Handbook of Georgia Boating Laws and Responsibilities, 'Navigation Rules -- Crossing Situations'

question: In an overtaking situation, which vessel is the give-way vessel?
choice_a: The vessel being overtaken must always yield to the faster, overtaking vessel
choice_b: Both vessels are stand-on vessels in an overtaking situation
choice_c: The vessel that is overtaking another vessel is always the give-way vessel; the vessel being overtaken is the stand-on vessel
choice_d: Whichever vessel is a sailboat is automatically the give-way vessel
explanation: When one vessel overtakes another, whether power-versus-power or power-versus-sail, the overtaking vessel is the give-way vessel and the vessel being overtaken is the stand-on vessel.
source_note: Handbook of Georgia Boating Laws and Responsibilities, 'Navigation Rules -- Overtaking'

question: When a powerboat encounters a sailboat under sail, which vessel is the give-way vessel?
choice_a: The sailboat must always give way to the powerboat
choice_b: Neither vessel needs to give way to the other
choice_c: The give-way vessel is determined by which one is larger
choice_d: The powerboat is the give-way vessel; the sailboat is the stand-on vessel
explanation: In a power-versus-sail encounter, the powerboat is the give-way vessel and the sailboat under sail is the stand-on vessel, unless the sailboat is overtaking the powerboat.
source_note: Handbook of Georgia Boating Laws and Responsibilities, 'Navigation Rules'

question: When operating a power-driven vessel in Georgia, to which vessels must you give way?
choice_a: Any vessel not under command, any vessel restricted in its ability to maneuver, a vessel engaged in commercial fishing, and a sailboat under sail unless it is overtaking
choice_b: Only to other power-driven vessels of the same size
choice_c: Only to vessels displaying an anchor light
choice_d: You never have to give way if you are the faster vessel
explanation: A power-driven vessel must give way to any vessel not under command, any vessel restricted in its ability to maneuver, vessels engaged in commercial fishing, and a sailboat under sail (unless the sailboat is overtaking).
source_note: Handbook of Georgia Boating Laws and Responsibilities, 'Encountering Vessels With Limited Maneuverability'

question: What does 'stand-on vessel' mean under Georgia's navigation rules?
choice_a: The vessel that must stop immediately
choice_b: The vessel that should maintain its course and speed
choice_c: The vessel that is anchored and not moving
choice_d: The vessel that has right-of-way regardless of the situation
explanation: The stand-on vessel is the one that should maintain its course and speed, while remaining alert in case the other operator does not take appropriate action.
source_note: Handbook of Georgia Boating Laws and Responsibilities, 'Navigation Rules'

question: What does 'give-way vessel' mean under Georgia's navigation rules?
choice_a: The vessel that always has priority to pass first
choice_b: The vessel that is required to sound its horn continuously
choice_c: The vessel that must take early and substantial action to avoid collision, such as stopping, slowing down, or changing course
choice_d: The vessel that must shut off its engine entirely
explanation: The give-way vessel is the one that must take early and substantial action -- stopping, slowing down, or changing course -- to avoid a collision.
source_note: Handbook of Georgia Boating Laws and Responsibilities, 'Navigation Rules'

question: When operating on a narrow river channel in Georgia, what should you do to operate safely and avoid collisions?
choice_a: Always travel in the exact center of the channel regardless of other traffic
choice_b: Cut corners at bends to save time and fuel
choice_c: Keep to the port (left) side of the channel at all times
choice_d: Keep as far to the starboard (right) side of the channel as is safe and practical, proceed with caution, and use appropriate sound signals near bends or when overtaking
explanation: On narrow river channels, operators should keep to the starboard side as far as safe and practical, proceed with caution and appropriate sound signals near bends or blind spots, and not cut corners.
source_note: Handbook of Georgia Boating Laws and Responsibilities, 'Operating in Narrow River Channels'

question: Under Georgia's rule for vessels under sail, to which vessels must a sailboat operator give way?
choice_a: Any vessel not under command, any vessel restricted in its ability to maneuver, and a vessel engaged in commercial fishing
choice_b: A sailboat under sail must give way to every power-driven vessel it encounters
choice_c: A sailboat under sail is never required to give way to anything
choice_d: Only to other sailboats of a larger size
explanation: Even a vessel operating under sail must give way to a vessel not under command, a vessel restricted in its ability to maneuver, and a vessel engaged in commercial fishing.
source_note: Handbook of Georgia Boating Laws and Responsibilities, 'Encountering Vessels With Limited Maneuverability'
